text: Azimuthal angular decorrelation of dijet systems provides a sensitive probe of QCD radiation patterns and of parton dynamics at small Bjorken x. This paper presents a study of jet azimuthal decorrelation in deep inelastic electron–proton scattering at the proposed Future Circular Collider in electron–proton mode (FCC-ep), in which a 60 GeV electron beam collides with a 50 TeV proton beam at a centre-of-mass energy of approximately 3.5 TeV. Simulated events are generated with leading-order and next-to-leading-order matrix elements matched to parton showers, and jets are reconstructed using the anti-kT algorithm within a realistic detector acceptance. The distribution of the azimuthal angle difference between the two leading jets is measured as a function of jet transverse momentum, photon virtuality, and rapidity separation. A clear decorrelation is observed, increasing with rapidity separation, and its magnitude is compared with predictions based on DGLAP and BFKL evolution. The results demonstrate that FCC-ep will extend the accessible kinematic range by more than an order of magnitude relative to HERA, enabling stringent tests of small-x QCD dynamics and potential sensitivity to gluon saturation effects.

# Richard III Reburied in Leicester as Cumberbatch Reads Tribute

Five centuries after he fell at the Battle of Bosworth, King Richard III was finally laid to rest Thursday at Leicester Cathedral, in a service that blended medieval pageantry with modern celebrity.

The last Plantagenet king was killed in 1485 and buried hastily in the church of Leicester's Greyfriars friary. Over the centuries the site was built over and forgotten. Then, in 2012, archaeologists sensationally rediscovered his remains beneath a city council car park, a find later confirmed by DNA testing against descendants of his sister.

On Thursday, 530 years after his death, the king's oak coffin was lowered into its grave inside the cathedral. Among those taking part was actor Benedict Cumberbatch, a distant cousin of Richard, who read a poem written for the occasion by Poet Laureate Carol Ann Duffy.

Philippa Langley, the historian whose campaign launched the search for the grave, said the discovery had prompted researchers to rethink the king. For centuries, Richard's reputation has been shaped largely by Tudor chroniclers and by Shakespeare, who portrayed him as a hunchbacked tyrant who murdered his young nephews, the "Princes in the Tower," to seize the crown.

Analysis of the skeleton showed that Richard had severe scoliosis but no withered arm, and that he suffered a fatal blow to the skull, grim evidence of his violent final moments on the battlefield.

For Leicester, the ceremony closes an extraordinary chapter. For historians, the argument over who Richard really was appears far from settled.

**Peterson Reinstated by NFL, Vikings Welcome Running Back's Return**

Minnesota Vikings running back Adrian Peterson has been reinstated by the National Football League, ending a suspension that followed his guilty plea to misdemeanor reckless assault in a child abuse case.

In announcing the decision, NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell made clear that Peterson's return comes with conditions. The league will require Peterson to continue attending counseling and to keep up with other treatment programs as part of his reinstatement. Failure to meet those obligations could lead to further discipline.

Peterson, one of the most accomplished rushers of his generation, was sidelined for nearly all of last season after he was charged in connection with the discipline of his young son. He later reached a plea agreement on the reduced misdemeanor charge, avoiding jail time. The league subsequently suspended him without pay, a decision Peterson and the NFL Players Association challenged.

The Vikings, who finished 7-9 last season without their star running back, responded to the news with a short statement saying they look forward to Peterson rejoining the team. The organization did not elaborate on how quickly he would be integrated into offseason activities.

The reinstatement raises questions about Peterson's future in Minnesota. His relationship with the club was reported to be strained during the suspension, and there has been ongoing speculation about whether he would prefer a fresh start elsewhere. He remains under contract with the Vikings.

At his peak, Peterson was the league's Most Valuable Player and nearly broke the single-season rushing record. Whether he can return to that level after a year away from the field, and at an age when many running backs begin to decline, remains to be seen.

For now, the Vikings say they are ready to have him back.

Claims such as "four out of five dentists recommend" are typically based on genuine surveys, but the wording often overstates what was actually measured. A company or its research contractor may poll a sample of dental professionals, sometimes a few hundred, and ask which brands they would recommend. Crucially, respondents are frequently permitted to name several brands. Consequently, 80 percent of dentists may include a particular toothpaste on their list while recommending competitors just as often.

In 2007, the UK Advertising Standards Authority ruled that a Colgate advertisement using this type of claim was misleading for precisely this reason. The statistic, therefore, does not usually mean that dentists prefer your toothpaste over all others. It generally indicates only that most surveyed dentists consider it an acceptable option, which is true of most fluoride toothpastes.

It happened on a Tuesday, in the cereal aisle of a Kroger in Dayton, Ohio.

I was holding a box of bran flakes, reading the fiber content, when it came back to me all at once. Not a voice. Not a vision. Just the plain recollection, the way you suddenly remember where you left your keys. Oh, right. I made all of this.

The bran flakes. The fluorescent lights humming overhead. The teenage stock boy with a cold sore, restocking the oatmeal. The oats themselves, the fields they grew in, the bees that worked those fields, the sun the bees flew under, the hundred billion other suns, and the dark that held them. I remembered deciding on the dark. It had seemed important at the time, to give things somewhere to be lonely.

I remembered all of it. Every sparrow, as the saying goes, though the saying undersells it. I remembered the sparrows' lice. I remembered the bacteria in the lice.

And I remembered everything that was happening, right now, everywhere.

That was the problem.

Because when you are God, you do not get to look away. I could feel a woman in Jakarta going into labor, and a man in Lisbon realizing his marriage was over, and a boy in Manitoba falling through the ice on a pond, and I knew, with the same terrible clarity, how each of those stories would end. I knew which ones I could change. I knew why I had decided, long ago, not to.

I had reasons. They were good reasons. I could feel how good they were, like load-bearing walls in a house. Free will. Consequence. The need for a world that is truly a world and not a puppet show. But reasons are cold comfort when you are holding a drowning boy in one part of your mind and a box of bran flakes in the other.

The stock boy looked over at me. "You okay, sir?"

I realized I was crying.

"Fine," I said. "Allergies."

He nodded and went back to the oatmeal. I knew his name was Tyler. I knew he would become a nurse. I knew the exact date he would die, and that it would be peaceful, and that his granddaughter would be holding his hand. I loved him so much that it bent my knees.

I put the bran flakes back on the shelf.

Here is the thing nobody tells you about omniscience: it is not knowledge. It is weight. Every grief in the universe arriving at once, all of it yours, because you are the one who made the room it happens in.

I understood, then, why I had done what I did. Why I had folded myself up so small and climbed inside a man named Gerald Pruitt, forty-seven, regional insurance adjuster, mild sleep apnea. It wasn't a punishment, and it wasn't an experiment. It was a vacation. It was the only way to rest.

So I did what any sensible person does with a memory too big to carry. I let go of it. I concentrated on the hum of the lights. On the squeak of my cart's bad wheel. On whether we needed milk. I felt the boy in Manitoba slip away from me, then the woman in Jakarta, then the suns, then the dark. It went faster than you would think. Forgetting is easy when you want it badly enough.

By the time I reached the dairy section, I was just Gerald again.

I bought the milk. I drove home. My wife asked how the store was, and I said fine, a little crowded, and she said that was Tuesdays for you.

That night I dreamed of a frozen pond, and woke up not knowing why my face was wet. I lay there in the dark for a long time, listening to my wife breathe, feeling grateful for something I couldn't name.

Then I went back to sleep. It's the one thing I've always been good at.

The sky did not darken. That was the cruel part. Everyone who had eyes knew the sun was still up there on the morning of the Blanking, warm on their faces, and none of them could see it.

It happened at 10:14 a.m. Eastern, simultaneously everywhere on Earth. Planes stayed in the air only because autopilot doesn't need eyes. Cars did not. By noon the hospitals were overwhelmed, and the doctors in them were as helpless as their patients.

Marguerite Oyelaran had been blind since she was six. On the morning of the Blanking she was making coffee in her apartment in Baltimore, and she noticed nothing at all until her neighbor started screaming.

She went next door, guided by the sound, and found him on his kitchen floor, crawling, knocking things over. She knelt beside him and took his hand.

"Mr. Kowalski," she said. "Stop moving. Breathe. You're going to learn this."

That was the first lesson. There would be millions more.

Within a week, the world's roughly forty million blind people had become the only functioning population on the planet. They knew how to cross streets by the sound of traffic. They knew how to read with their fingers, how to cook without burning themselves, how to count money by its fold. They had spent their lives navigating a world built for the sighted. Now the sighted needed to be navigated.

Marguerite, who had been a mid-level employee at the National Federation of the Blind, found herself at the head of something like a government by the end of the month. It wasn't elected. There wasn't time. The blind organized because they were the only ones who could, and people followed whoever had a calm voice and a plan.

Her plan was simple: teach. Every blind person would take ten sighted students. Those students, once competent, would teach ten more. Cane technique first. Then braille. Then cooking, cleaning, the thousand tiny skills of daily life.

It worked better than anyone expected, partly because the newly blind were so desperate, and partly because their teachers were patient in a way that only people who had spent decades being underestimated could be.

Not everyone accepted it. In the second year, a movement rose among the formerly sighted, led by a former senator, demanding a "return to normal governance." They wanted their old leaders back. They wanted the institutions that had run things before.

Marguerite met him in a town hall packed with people. She could hear them breathing, shifting, the rustle of anxiety.

"Senator," she said, "who taught you to tie your shoes again?"

He was quiet.

"Who taught your wife to cook? Who taught your grandchildren to read?" She let the silence sit. "You can have your old institutions. But they were built by people who never once thought about us. We had to build our own. That's why we were ready, and you weren't."

The movement didn't disappear, but it shrank. People were tired, and they had learned something difficult about who had been invisible in the old world.

Years later, scientists still had no explanation for the Blanking. Some of the sighted still prayed every night to wake up and see.

Marguerite didn't blame them. But she had a different hope. She hoped that if sight ever returned, the world would remember who had taken its hand when it was crawling on the kitchen floor.

Plants have no nervous system, no brain, and no way to move from place to place, yet they constantly sense their surroundings and adjust their behavior in response. Over the past few decades, researchers have found that plants exchange information both within their own bodies and with other organisms through several channels. The word "communication" is used loosely here: it means sending and receiving signals that change behavior, not conscious intention.

## Communication Within a Single Plant

**Electrical signals.** When a leaf is wounded, electrical changes in membrane potential can travel to distant parts of the plant within seconds to minutes. In a widely cited 2018 study, Toyota and colleagues used a fluorescent calcium sensor in *Arabidopsis* to show waves of calcium moving from a caterpillar-damaged leaf to other leaves, triggering defense responses. The Venus flytrap is the most dramatic example: two touches to its trigger hairs within about 20 seconds generate action potentials that snap the trap shut.

**Hormonal signals.** Plant hormones such as jasmonic acid, salicylic acid, ethylene, and auxin coordinate growth and defense across tissues. Damage in one leaf can lead to jasmonate-driven production of defensive compounds throughout the plant, a phenomenon called systemic acquired resistance (or, for wound responses, systemic induced resistance).

**Hydraulic signals.** Changes in water pressure can also travel quickly through the vascular system and influence processes like stomatal closure.

## Communication Between Plants

**Airborne chemicals (volatile organic compounds).** This is the best-supported form of plant-to-plant signaling.

- In the 1980s, researchers reported that willow and poplar trees near insect-damaged neighbors increased their own chemical defenses. These early studies were criticized for their methods but sparked a field of research.
- Later, stronger work came from sagebrush and wild tobacco. Richard Karban's field experiments showed that clipping sagebrush released volatiles that made nearby plants (including tobacco) suffer less herbivore damage.
- Lima beans exposed to volatiles from damaged neighbors produce more extrafloral nectar, which attracts predatory insects.
- Green leaf volatiles, the "cut grass" smell, are released almost instantly upon damage and can prime defenses in neighboring plants.

**Root exudates.** Plants release chemicals from their roots that affect neighbors. Some suppress competitors (allelopathy, as in black walnut's juglone). Others appear to help plants recognize kin; studies on sea rocket (*Cakile edentula*) found that plants grew fewer competitive roots when sharing soil with siblings than with strangers.

**Mycorrhizal networks.** Most plants partner with fungi that colonize their roots, and fungal threads can connect multiple plants underground. Experiments in the 1990s by Suzanne Simard and colleagues tracked carbon isotopes moving between trees through these networks, and later lab work suggested that defense signals could travel between connected plants. This idea, often called the "wood wide web," is popular but contested. A 2023 review by Karst, Jones, and Hoeksema argued that field evidence for widespread resource sharing and "mother trees" nurturing seedlings is much weaker than public accounts suggest. Fungal networks clearly exist; how much they function as communication systems is still debated.

## Communication With Other Species

Plants also send signals to animals and microbes:

- **Calling bodyguards:** Corn attacked by caterpillars releases volatiles that attract parasitic wasps, which lay eggs inside the caterpillars.
- **Attracting pollinators:** Flower color, scent, ultraviolet patterns, and even electric fields help guide bees. Some research suggests bumblebees can detect floral electric charges.
- **Recruiting microbes:** Under stress, roots can change their exudates to recruit beneficial bacteria.

## Sensing and Responding

Plants also "listen." Studies have shown that *Arabidopsis* exposed to recordings of caterpillar chewing vibrations later produced more defensive chemicals than plants exposed to silence or wind sounds. Roots of pea plants have been reported to grow toward the sound of running water, though such findings need further replication.

## How Strong Is the Evidence?

| Mechanism | Strength of evidence |
|---|---|
| Internal electrical, hormonal, hydraulic signaling | Strong |
| Airborne volatiles between plants | Strong, especially in lab and some field settings |
| Signals to insects and pollinators | Strong |
| Root-based kin recognition | Moderate |
| Mycorrhizal "communication" and resource sharing | Debated; real but probably overstated |
| Plant "hearing" | Early and intriguing |

## Bottom Line

Plants coordinate their behavior through electrical, chemical, and hydraulic signals, and they exchange chemical information with neighbors, insects, and microbes. These processes are well documented and help plants defend themselves, compete, and reproduce. Claims that plants are "intelligent" or that forests act as cooperative superorganisms go beyond the evidence, but the core finding is solid: plants are far more responsive and interconnected than they appear.

# How to Make a Great Texas-Style Smoked Brisket

Texas brisket is famously simple on paper: beef, salt, pepper, smoke, and time. The difficulty lies in executing each step well over a cook that can last 12 hours or more. Here's how to do it right.

## 1. Choose the Right Brisket

Buy a **whole packer brisket**, which includes both the lean "flat" and the fattier "point." Aim for 12 to 16 pounds. Grade matters: USDA Prime or high Choice has more intramuscular fat, which makes the meat more forgiving. When you pick it up, a good brisket should bend a little in the middle; a stiff one is often tougher.

## 2. Trim Carefully

Trimming shapes how the brisket cooks.

- Chill the brisket first; cold fat is easier to cut.
- Trim the fat cap down to about **¼ inch**. Too much fat won't render and blocks the bark from forming; too little leaves the meat exposed.
- Remove the hard, waxy fat between the point and the flat (the "deckle") where you can reach it.
- Round off thin edges and corners so they don't burn.
- Square up the flat so it's an even thickness from end to end.

Keep the trimmings. You can render them into tallow for later.

## 3. Season Like Central Texas

The classic rub is just **coarse kosher salt and 16-mesh black pepper**, usually in equal parts by volume. Some pitmasters add a little garlic powder, but purists stick to salt and pepper. Apply an even coat on all sides. If you like, use a thin layer of mustard or hot sauce as a binder, though it isn't necessary. Season an hour before cooking or the night before.

## 4. Set Up Your Smoker

An offset smoker is traditional, but pellet grills, kamados, and kettles set up for indirect heat all work.

- **Wood:** Post oak is the Texas standard. Hickory or pecan are good alternatives. Avoid mesquite for long cooks; it can turn bitter.
- **Temperature:** Hold steady at **225–275°F**. Many pitmasters aim for around 250°F.
- **Smoke:** You want thin, blue, barely visible smoke. Thick white smoke means the fire is smoldering and will coat the meat in a sooty, acrid flavor.

Place a water pan in the cooker to help maintain humidity and stabilize temperature.

## 5. The Cook

Put the brisket on the grate **fat side up or down** depending on your smoker. In offsets where heat comes from one side, many cooks place the point toward the firebox, since it can handle more heat.

Leave it alone for the first several hours. Spritz with water, apple cider vinegar, or beef broth every hour or so after the bark has set (around hour three) if the surface looks dry.

## 6. Beat the Stall

Somewhere around **150–170°F internal**, the temperature will stop climbing, sometimes for hours. This is evaporative cooling. You have two choices:

- **Push through** unwrapped for maximum bark.
- **Wrap** in pink butcher paper (the "Texas crutch") once the bark is a deep mahogany color and doesn't rub off when touched. Butcher paper breathes better than foil, so it preserves more bark while speeding up the cook. Some people add a smear of beef tallow before wrapping.

## 7. Cook to Tenderness, Not a Number

Brisket is usually done between **200 and 205°F**, but temperature is only a guide. The real test is feel: a probe or skewer should slide into the thickest part of the flat with almost no resistance, like pushing into soft butter. Check several spots. If any area feels tight, keep cooking.

## 8. Rest It

Resting is non-negotiable. Pull the brisket, leave it wrapped, and let it rest **at least one hour**, ideally two to four. Wrap the whole package in towels and place it in an empty cooler, or hold it in an oven set to around 150–170°F. Resting lets the juices redistribute and the connective tissue finish relaxing.

## 9. Slice It Properly

- Separate the point from the flat along the fat seam.
- Slice the **flat against the grain** into pencil-thick slices, about ¼ inch.
- Turn the point 90 degrees (its grain runs differently) and slice it slightly thicker, or cube it for burnt ends.

A perfectly cooked slice should hold together when lifted but pull apart with a gentle tug.

## 10. Serve Simply

In Texas, brisket comes on butcher paper with white bread, pickles, raw onion, and maybe sauce on the side. If you've done everything right, you won't need the sauce.

## Quick Tips

- Buy a good leave-in thermometer for both the meat and the pit.
- Plan for roughly **1 to 1.5 hours per pound**, then add time for resting. Start earlier than you think.
- Keep notes on each cook. Brisket rewards practice more than any single recipe.

Both, really. The Romans borrowed openly from Greece, and they knew it: Horace wrote that "captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive." But they also contributed plenty that was genuinely their own:

- **Law:** A systematic legal tradition with professional jurists and concepts of contracts, property, and citizens' rights that still underpins civil law across Europe and Latin America.
- **Engineering:** Concrete construction that made vast vaults and domes like the Pantheon possible, plus aqueducts, sewers, and a road network spanning the Mediterranean.
- **Governance:** Running a multiethnic empire for centuries while gradually extending citizenship to conquered peoples.
- **Literature and art:** Verse satire, which Quintilian proudly called "wholly ours," and a distinctive tradition of unflinchingly realistic portrait busts.

Besides, Greek culture itself drew heavily on Egypt and the Near East. Borrowing and adapting is how civilizations normally develop.

Deaths and Jailings of Putin Critics Raise Suspicions; Kremlin Rejects Claims

MOSCOW — For many of Vladimir Putin's opponents, speaking out against the Russian president has come at a steep price. Over the past two decades, a string of critics, journalists and political rivals have been shot, poisoned or sent to prison, a pattern that human rights groups and Western governments say cannot be explained by chance.

The Kremlin rejects that interpretation outright, insisting it has no role in the deaths and that those imprisoned were convicted of genuine crimes in Russian courts.

The most recent case to draw international attention was the killing of Boris Nemtsov, a former deputy prime minister and outspoken opposition leader who was shot dead on a bridge within sight of the Kremlin walls. Nemtsov had been working on a report about Russian military involvement in eastern Ukraine at the time of his death. Several men from Chechnya were arrested and later convicted, but Nemtsov's allies say the people who ordered the killing have never been identified.

His death followed a long list of similar cases. Investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, a fierce critic of Russia's war in Chechnya, was shot in the elevator of her Moscow apartment building in 2006. That same year, former security officer Alexander Litvinenko died in London after being poisoned with radioactive polonium-210. A British public inquiry later concluded that his killing was "probably approved" by Putin, a finding Moscow dismissed as politically motivated.

Others have faced prison rather than violence. Former oil tycoon Mikhail Khodorkovsky, once Russia's richest man, spent a decade behind bars on fraud and tax evasion charges that his supporters called retribution for funding the opposition. Anti-corruption campaigner Alexei Navalny was repeatedly arrested and convicted in cases widely condemned abroad as politically driven.

"There is a clear message being sent," said one Moscow-based human rights advocate, who asked not to be named out of concern for her safety. "Not every critic is killed, but everyone knows it could happen."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has repeatedly described such accusations as baseless. Officials argue that Russia has an independent justice system, that many of the cases were thoroughly investigated, and that Western governments and media use the deaths to smear the country. Putin himself has suggested that some killings may have been staged by his enemies to make the Russian government look bad.

Analysts note that proving direct state involvement is extremely difficult. Investigations are controlled by Russian authorities, and those convicted are often low-level suspects. That ambiguity, critics say, is part of the point: it allows officials to deny responsibility while the climate of fear does its work.

For now, Russia's opposition remains small and fragmented. Many of its most prominent figures have either left the country or are in prison, and those who remain say they weigh the risks every time they speak in public.

In my last life I was Gerald Pruitt, certified public accountant, and I died at my desk on April 14th, which is the least surprising way an accountant has ever gone.

For sixty-eight years, I was agreeable. I laughed at my boss's golf stories. I told my sister-in-law her tuna casserole was "really something." I said "no, no, after you" to men who deserved to wait in the rain. Then I closed my eyes over a stack of tax returns and opened them in a hospital nursery, red-faced and furious and named Tyler, with every memory intact.

It took me a while to appreciate what I'd been given. Not the knowledge. The immunity. Nobody holds a small child responsible for anything. It took five agonizing years to get my mouth working properly, and I have been making up for lost time ever since.

At Aunt Denise's wedding, in that holy hush right before the vows, I tugged my mother's sleeve and asked, at a volume calibrated to reach the back pew, "Mommy, when they get divorced, who gets the boat?"

At Grandpa Lou's funeral, the pastor invited anyone with a memory to come forward. I raised my hand. "Grandpa always said he didn't trust banks," I told the congregation, "so is the money still in the freezer, or did somebody already check?" Three of my uncles slipped out before the final hymn. Only two came back.

When Dad had his regional manager over for pot roast, I waited until the man's mouth was full, then asked whether golden parachutes were only for the people who do the firing, and whether Daddy would get a parachute too or just the push.

At the mall, I climbed onto Santa's lap and asked for a Roth IRA. "Mommy says it's too late for her," I explained, "but I've still got time for compound interest to work." Santa, who I'd estimate was sixty-one and renting, needed a moment.

In Sunday school, Mrs. Abernathy asked what God wants from us. "Ten percent," I said. "But is that gross or net?"

My parents have had me evaluated twice. The first psychologist called me gifted. The second asked, very carefully, whether anyone in the household worked in accounting.

I know what you're thinking. With a CPA's brain in a six-year-old's body, I could be a prodigy. Morning television. College at eleven. Instead, I'm the kid who asked a pregnant stranger at Target whether she was planning to claim it as a dependent this year.

But I've already lived the sensible life. It got me a corner office, a retirement party I didn't survive long enough to attend, and a coronary in the middle of tax season.

Tonight, Mom tucked me in and asked, in the voice of a woman at the very end of her rope, where I learn these things. I gave her my roundest, most innocent eyes.

"Mommy," I whispered, "what's a midlife crisis, and why does Daddy's new car have one?"

A fractal is a geometric object that displays self-similarity, meaning that its parts resemble the whole at different scales of magnification, and whose complexity is measured by a fractional, or non-integer, dimension. Although fractals began as abstract constructions in pure mathematics, Benoit Mandelbrot argued in *The Fractal Geometry of Nature* (1982) that they describe many natural forms more faithfully than the smooth figures of Euclidean geometry. Clouds, as he observed, are not spheres, and mountains are not cones.

Coastlines offer the classic illustration. Because a coastline is irregular at every scale, its measured length increases as the measuring unit becomes smaller, a result known as the coastline paradox. Fractal dimension provides a more meaningful description than length alone; the west coast of Great Britain, for example, has a dimension of approximately 1.25.

Living systems frequently adopt fractal architectures because such structures maximize surface area or coverage within a limited volume. The branching of the human airways and blood vessels, like that of trees and root systems, enables the efficient exchange and distribution of gases, fluids, and nutrients.

Fractal patterns also emerge from physical processes, as seen in lightning discharges, mineral dendrites, river networks shaped by erosion, turbulent flow, and the strange attractors that characterize chaotic systems such as atmospheric convection.

It should be noted, however, that physical fractals are approximations. Their self-similarity is typically statistical rather than exact and holds only across a limited range of scales. Even so, the concept has considerable practical value in antenna design, materials science, and computer graphics.

Population atlases of brain and spinal cord anatomy are essential for spatial normalization, morphometric analysis, and the study of neurological disease, yet most existing atlases treat the brain and spinal cord separately and are built with deterministic registration that offers limited insight into anatomical variability. We present a generative framework for diffeomorphic atlas construction that jointly models the brain and cervical spinal cord from MRI data. The method represents each subject as a smooth, invertible deformation of a shared template and learns both the template and a probabilistic model of deformations within a variational inference setting, implemented with a convolutional neural network. This formulation enables efficient registration of new subjects, sampling of plausible anatomical variants, and quantification of uncertainty in the estimated deformations. We evaluate the approach on multi-subject T1- and T2-weighted MRI datasets, demonstrating improved alignment of anatomical structures, preserved topology, and substantially reduced computation time compared with conventional iterative atlas-building methods.

A standard chessboard has **64** squares if you count only the individual light and dark squares. If you count every square that can be traced on the board, including larger squares made up of smaller ones, the answer is **204**.

## Counting squares of every size

In addition to the 1 × 1 squares, the 8 × 8 grid contains 2 × 2 squares, 3 × 3 squares, and so on, up to the entire board, which is itself one 8 × 8 square. The key is to count how many positions each size can occupy.

Take a 2 × 2 square. Its top-left corner can sit in any of the first 7 columns and any of the first 7 rows, so there are 7 × 7 = 49 of them. In general, a k × k square fits in (9 − k)² positions:

| Square size | How many |
|---|---|
| 1 × 1 | 8² = 64 |
| 2 × 2 | 7² = 49 |
| 3 × 3 | 6² = 36 |
| 4 × 4 | 5² = 25 |
| 5 × 5 | 4² = 16 |
| 6 × 6 | 3² = 9 |
| 7 × 7 | 2² = 4 |
| 8 × 8 | 1² = 1 |
| **Total** | **204** |

## The general formula

The total is the sum of the first eight perfect squares, and there's a well-known formula for the sum of the first n squares:

1² + 2² + 3² + ... + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6

With n = 8, this gives (8 × 9 × 17) / 6 = 1,224 / 6 = 204, matching the table. The formula works for any square grid. A 3 × 3 tic-tac-toe board, for example, has 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 squares.

## Going further: rectangles

The puzzle is sometimes extended to rectangles. Every rectangle on the board is defined by picking two of the 9 horizontal grid lines and two of the 9 vertical grid lines. There are C(9, 2) = 36 ways to choose each pair, so the board contains 36 × 36 = **1,296** rectangles, 204 of which are squares.

## Summary

- **64** individual squares
- **204** squares of all sizes
- **1,296** rectangles of all sizes, squares included

The question is a classic precisely because most people stop at 64. For a complete answer, say which interpretation you're using and show the sum that leads to 204.

The Office on the Fourteenth Floor

Dr. Eleanor Vance maintained her practice in an unremarkable building downtown, between a dental surgery and an accounting firm. Her nameplate listed no specialty. Referrals arrived by word of mouth, through channels that she had learned not to question.

Her nine o'clock on Monday was a man who had once attempted to flood a coastal city. He sat in the armchair across from her, removed his gloves with deliberate care, and spoke for forty minutes about his father.

"He told me the ocean would take everything eventually," the man said. "I suppose I wished to prove him right on my own schedule."

Dr. Vance made a note. She did not write the word *villain* in her files. She had abandoned that term early in her career, after realizing it described an outcome rather than a person. Her clients had committed terrible acts; several remained capable of committing more. Her work was not to absolve them. It was to understand what had brought them to the threshold, and whether any of them might still be persuaded to step back.

At eleven, a young woman who called herself the Archivist arrived twelve minutes late and apologized four times. She had erased the memories of an entire town in pursuit of what she described as a cleaner history. In session, she was meticulous, anxious, and frightened of being forgotten herself. Dr. Vance observed, not for the first time, that grandiose ambitions frequently concealed very small and very old fears.

"Do you believe I can change?" the Archivist asked.

"I believe you are asking," Dr. Vance replied, "and that is not nothing."

Her afternoon client was the most difficult. He had no particular grievance, no wounded childhood that he would admit to, and no stated objective beyond what he termed "the elegance of collapse." He found the therapeutic process amusing and treated each session as a game of chess in which he was several moves ahead.

"You know what I am," he said. "Why continue?"

Dr. Vance considered the question with the seriousness it deserved. "Because you continue to come," she said. "No one compels you. Some part of you wants something from this room. I am patient enough to wait until you can tell me what it is."

He was silent for a long moment. Then he looked at the clock and stood. "Same time next week," he said, which was the closest he had ever come to an answer.

In the evenings, Dr. Vance wrote her case notes and then consulted with her own supervisor, a retired psychiatrist who reminded her, regularly, of the ethical limits of confidentiality and of her duty to warn when lives were at stake. She had invoked that duty twice. Both clients had returned afterward, which surprised her each time.

She did not consider herself brave. She considered herself a professional who had accepted an unusual caseload. Every person, she had come to believe, was the protagonist of their own account, however distorted. Her task was to sit with that account long enough to locate the first wrong turn.

Occasionally, she found it. Occasionally, the client turned back.

Those were the days she remembered, and the reason she kept the office on the fourteenth floor.

Convolutional neural networks owe much of their success on images to the regular grid structure and translation symmetry of the plane, neither of which exists on curved surfaces. A common workaround maps a surface to a planar domain and applies a standard CNN, but existing surface-to-image representations either introduce large area distortion or require several images to cover the whole shape. We propose a new representation for sphere-type surfaces based on general covering maps. Rather than relying on a toric cover with a fixed set of cone points, our construction lets a flat torus wrap around the surface several times, so that every region appears with low distortion somewhere in a single image. Because this image is seamless and periodic, convolution with circular padding is well defined, and off-the-shelf architectures apply with minimal modification. Predictions from the multiple copies of each surface point are then aggregated back onto the mesh. Experiments on shape segmentation and classification benchmarks show that the method matches or exceeds competing approaches while remaining simple and efficient.

Pop Culture Roundup: "Star Wars" Fans Get a Jolt, and a Reporter's Rant Goes Viral for All the Wrong Reasons

It was a week of extremes in entertainment news, with one long-awaited trailer sending fans into a frenzy and one short video clip sending a television reporter into damage-control mode. Here's a look at the stories that dominated conversation online.

**Han Solo is back**

The biggest moment of the week arrived when Lucasfilm unveiled the second teaser trailer for "Star Wars: The Force Awakens" at the Star Wars Celebration fan convention in Anaheim, California. Within hours, the two-minute preview had racked up millions of views and become the top trending topic on social media.

The trailer offered fleeting glimpses of new characters played by John Boyega, Daisy Ridley and Oscar Isaac, along with the wreckage of a Star Destroyer half-buried in desert sand. But the shot that sent fans over the edge came at the very end, when Harrison Ford appeared as Han Solo alongside Chewbacca and delivered a single line: "Chewie, we're home."

Fans who packed the convention hall reportedly screamed so loudly when Ford appeared that the audio was hard to hear. Director J.J. Abrams and producer Kathleen Kennedy took the stage to introduce the footage and were joined by members of the cast, including original stars Mark Hamill and Carrie Fisher.

The film, the first installment in a new trilogy, is scheduled to open in December.

**An apology after a meltdown**

On the other end of the spectrum, ESPN reporter Britt McHenry found herself at the center of a backlash after a video surfaced showing her berating an employee at a towing company in Virginia.

In the footage, which was recorded by a security camera and posted online, McHenry can be heard insulting the woman's appearance, education and job, telling her she was "on television" while the employee was not. The clip spread quickly, drawing widespread criticism from viewers who called her comments cruel and elitist.

ESPN announced that McHenry had been suspended for one week. McHenry apologized on Twitter, writing that she had allowed her emotions to get the better of her during "an intense and stressful moment" and that she was "embarrassed" by her behavior.

The episode set off a broader online debate about how people treat service workers, as well as how much a private moment caught on camera should affect someone's career.

**Elsewhere in entertainment**

The week also brought plenty of smaller buzz. Streaming services continued their push for original programming, a handful of networks announced which shows had been renewed or canceled ahead of the fall season, and festival lineups for the summer concert circuit continued to roll out, giving music fans plenty to plan around.

If this week proved anything, it's that the internet can turn a two-minute video into a global event, whether that video features a beloved space smuggler or a moment someone would surely rather forget.

**Boko Haram Pledges Allegiance to ISIS, but Analyst Sees Little Immediate Battlefield Change**

The Nigerian militant group Boko Haram has reportedly pledged its allegiance to ISIS, a move that formally links one of Africa's deadliest insurgencies with the extremist organization controlling large parts of Iraq and Syria.

The pledge appeared in an audio message attributed to Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau and posted online. In the recording, the speaker declares loyalty to ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi. The authenticity of the message could not be independently verified, though it follows months of growing signs that the two groups were moving closer, including increasingly similar propaganda and video production.

Boko Haram has waged a violent campaign in northeastern Nigeria for years, killing thousands of people and displacing well over a million. The group drew worldwide condemnation in 2014 after kidnapping more than 200 schoolgirls from the town of Chibok. In recent months, its attacks have spilled into neighboring Cameroon, Niger, and Chad, prompting a regional military offensive.

Despite the dramatic headline, at least one expert cautions against overstating the immediate significance. J. Peter Pham, director of the Atlantic Council's Africa Center, said that in the short term the alliance is unlikely to have a major impact on the battlefield. Boko Haram's fighters, tactics, and areas of operation will remain largely the same, and the two groups are separated by vast distances that make sharing fighters or weapons difficult.

Pham suggested that the pledge is more about branding and legitimacy. For Boko Haram, which is under mounting military pressure, aligning with ISIS could boost its profile and help with recruitment. For ISIS, the pledge offers a chance to claim expansion into West Africa.

Over the longer term, analysts warn, closer ties could bring Boko Haram greater access to funding, expertise, and propaganda resources, a development that would deepen concern among governments in the region and beyond.

Let T and S be commuting contractions on a Hilbert space H. A vector x is called a joint coboundary if it lies in the range of both I − T and I − S, and a double coboundary if it lies in the range of (I − T)(I − S). Every double coboundary is clearly a joint coboundary, and we study when the converse holds. We show that, in general, the inclusion is strict: there exist commuting unitary operators, and even commuting contractions arising from measure-preserving actions, for which some joint coboundaries fail to be double coboundaries. On the other hand, we obtain sufficient conditions, expressed through spectral properties and the closedness of the relevant ranges, under which the two notions coincide. Applications to the joint behavior of ergodic averages and to the solvability of coupled cohomological equations are discussed.
